clue.text: Drewsteignton oddly with Whitehall address

indicators.note: the letters are set out in an odd, strange way

explanation.surface: A Devon village is somehow tied up with the seat of government in London.
explanation.walkthrough: "Oddly" looks as if it wants the odd letters of Drewsteignton, a Dartmoor village; take them and you get DESEGTN, which is useless. Here it means strangely, so the whole name is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Downing Street runs off Whitehall and is home to the Prime Minister, so it is literally an address there.

clue.text: Like a stop sign a lot can go out of shape

indicators.note: the letters lose their form and take a new one

explanation.surface: A remark that a car park or a plot of land can get bent out of shape.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator folds the letters' own verb into itself: "can go" is fodder, and "go out of shape" reuses nothing, since "go" appears twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: a stop sign is an eight-sided plate, and eight-sided is what the answer means.

clue.text: Group not heartless, embracing individual

indicators.note: the heart, the middle letter, is taken away
the outer letters hug the inner piece

explanation.surface: A group insists it is not cold-hearted, since it takes care of an individual member.
explanation.walkthrough: "Heartless" looks like a description of the group; it is an instruction on "not", and "individual" is simply one.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonet is a group of nine, usually musicians.

clue.text: Pries into one’s new suit first

indicators.note: the letters are made new, put in a fresh order

explanation.surface: Someone snoops into another person's brand-new suit before anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: "Pries into" reads as one phrase, but only "Pries" is the definition; "into" just joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To nose is to pry, so someone who noses about pries.

clue.text: Group supplying material to newspapers announces two girls

explanation.surface: A press agency makes an announcement about two young women.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is long and reads like a dictionary entry, which hides that the whole back half is just two first names.
explanation.definitionFit: A syndicate is an agency that sells articles and features to many newspapers at once.

clue.text: Criticise complaint at Sunday lunch

blocks.note: to roast someone is to criticise them harshly

explanation.surface: Someone moans and finds fault over the family meal on a Sunday.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a grumbler at the table; the two verbs of complaint turn out to be the meal itself. Roast beef is the traditional British Sunday lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the traditional British Sunday lunch is a roast, and this joint is its best-known form.

clue.text: Communication of some parliamentary upset

indicators.note: only part of the next word is used
in a down clue, upset turns the letters upside down, so they read backwards

explanation.surface: A message about some trouble in Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: "Upset" looks like the political mood; in a down clue it tells you to read the hidden letters from bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: An email is a message sent electronically, a form of communication.

clue.text: How hands move 24/7?

blocks.note: a clock's hands travel round its face

explanation.surface: A question about how workers' hands keep busy all day and every day.
explanation.walkthrough: "Hands" reads as workers on a non-stop shift; they are the hands of a clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Clock hands move round the clock, and round the clock also means continuously, 24/7.

clue.text: South African boy making smoother mayonnaise

blocks.note: initials of South Africa, used as an adjective here
to dress stone or timber is to smooth it

explanation.surface: A young South African whisks mayonnaise until it is silky.
explanation.walkthrough: "Making smoother" sounds like the whisking; it is dressing, the old sense of finishing a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: mayonnaise is one member of the wider class the answer names.

clue.text: I go nuts arranging day trips

indicators.note: the letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: An organiser complains that planning day trips drives them mad.
explanation.walkthrough: "I go nuts" sounds like a cry of frustration, but it supplies every letter; "arranging" belongs with it, not with the trips.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: excursions made for pleasure, usually lasting a day.

clue.text: Falls again, turning back with artist

indicators.note: the word is turned round to face the other way

explanation.surface: Someone takes another tumble, turning back to be with a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: "Falls" reads as a verb, someone falling again; it is the noun, the waterfall.
explanation.definitionFit: Niagara is the name of the famous Falls on the US-Canada border.

clue.text: The dark man on board, it’s said

indicators.note: what is spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: a knight is a chess piece

explanation.surface: Talk of a sinister figure aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: "Man on board" suggests a sailor; it is a chessman on a chessboard.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: "the dark" as a noun is the time after sunset, when the sun is down.

clue.text: Very minor piece composed, it’s all in C

indicators.note: the letters are put together in a new way

explanation.surface: A short piece of music has been written, entirely in the key of C.
explanation.walkthrough: "Minor", "piece", "composed" and "C" all point at music, yet the answer is just a tiny amount.
explanation.definitionFit: A scintilla is a tiny trace or particle.

clue.text: Heavyweight in charge of drink

blocks.note: a ton is a great weight

explanation.surface: A heavyweight boxer runs the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: IC for "in charge" is a standard abbreviation, and a ton is the heavyweight unit; "of" merely links.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym for one kind of drink: the quinine mixer that goes with gin.

clue.text: Revoked, when intoxicated in prison room? Quite the opposite

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other
swap the roles just described

blocks.note: caned is British slang for very drunk or high
a cell is a room in a prison

explanation.surface: A privilege is withdrawn when a prisoner is found drunk in his cell.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally the clue puts intoxicated inside prison room; "Quite the opposite" swaps them, so the prison room goes inside. Caned is British slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: an order or licence that is revoked has been called off.

clue.text: Newly canonised, very quickly

indicators.note: the letters are made new, into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A saint is made in an unusually swift ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a fast-track sainthood; the comma splits the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: In a second means almost instantly, very quickly.

clue.text: I can go on about English drifter

blocks.note: to go on about something is to rant

explanation.surface: A wanderer boasts of being able to talk at length about English.
explanation.walkthrough: "I can" reads as a boast; it is two pieces, I and a tin. The E is slotted in before RANT, not after it as the clue order would suggest.
explanation.definitionFit: An itinerant travels from place to place, as a drifter does.

clue.text: Vieux?

blocks.note: the surface offers a lone French word, as if asking for its translation
the question mark warns the answer describes the word itself: what language, and what it means

explanation.walkthrough: Two readings stack: vieux is French for old, and Old French is the medieval language itself, so the answer both translates and labels the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Vieux means old in French, so the word is literally 'old' in French.

clue.text: For instance, worker in business producing plant

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

explanation.surface: A worker in a company producing plants, perhaps in horticulture.
explanation.walkthrough: "Business" suggests a firm; here it is a line of work, and "worker" is the crossword's standard ant.
explanation.definitionFit: Eglantine is the sweetbriar, a wild rose.

clue.text: Ineffectual compromise that a confectioner provides

blocks.note: a deal that blurs the issue rather than settling it
a soft sweet made from sugar, butter and milk

explanation.surface: A weak deal is struck, the sort of thing a sweet-maker would hand out.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves read as one sentence about a deal, but they split at "that": a political dodge and a sweet share one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A fudge is a vague compromise that dodges the issue, and also a soft sweet.

clue.text: Old BBC magazine’s ears?

blocks.note: The Listener, a BBC weekly, closed in 1991
ears are what we listen with

explanation.surface: A question about the ears of a former BBC publication.
explanation.walkthrough: The Listener was a weekly magazine the BBC published until 1991; its possessive, Listener's, is spelt as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ears are listeners in a playful sense, the organs that listen.

clue.text: Meal for Passover some organised erroneously

indicators.note: only part of the words is taken

explanation.surface: Some people arranged the Passover meal badly.
explanation.walkthrough: "Erroneously" looks like an anagram signal for "some organised"; it is only there to carry the last three letters, and "some" does the work.
explanation.definitionFit: The Seder is the ritual meal on the first night or nights of Passover.

clue.text: Delicacy from his US cooking

indicators.note: the letters are worked over into a new form

explanation.surface: A treat comes out of some American man's kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that "cooking" makes sushi, which is famously not cooked.
explanation.definitionFit: Sushi is a Japanese delicacy of vinegared rice and raw fish.

clue.text: Sweetheart in saloons worries

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a saloon is a car with a separate boot
the heart, middle letter, of sweet

explanation.surface: A lover in Wild West bars has troubles.
explanation.walkthrough: Saloons suggest bars; in Britain a saloon is a car body style, what Americans call a sedan. E goes inside CARS.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: cares as a plural noun are anxieties, the things one worries about.

clue.text: Goldfinches in a group delight

blocks.note: the collective noun for goldfinches, like a murder of crows

explanation.surface: Goldfinches flocking together are a joy to see.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, goldfinches in a group bring delight; the setter splits it after "group", and the collective noun for goldfinches is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: a collective-noun sense unique to goldfinches, and the ordinary verb meaning to please or enchant.

clue.text: Cover turned back in fancy lace – as seen in Façade

indicators.note: something turned back is folded over the other way, so the word reads in reverse
one piece goes inside the other
the letters are fancifully rearranged

explanation.surface: A cloth folded back to show lace, as in Façade, the Edith Sitwell poems.
explanation.walkthrough: Façade is italicised because it is a title, Edith Sitwell's sequence of poems; the definition works by example, pointing at the mark under its c.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the little hook under the c of Façade is the mark the answer names.

clue.text: Quiet before long consumes northern river and sea area

indicators.note: one piece swallows the other

explanation.surface: A calm spell will soon swallow the north, like a shipping forecast.
explanation.walkthrough: "Consumes" sits between two ideas of time, so it is easy to miss that it is the container signal. Shannon is Ireland's longest river and a sea area in the BBC Shipping Forecast.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shannon is Ireland's longest river and also a Shipping Forecast sea area.

clue.text: French landmark damaged car he imported

indicators.note: the letters are knocked out of shape

explanation.surface: A Paris monument is hit by a car a man brought in from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a traffic accident, fittingly, since the Arc sits in the middle of a notorious roundabout.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arc de Triomphe is the triumphal arch in Paris.
